reason: The sources provide 22 cross-verified facts detailing STS-1's launch shockwave crisis, tile loss, and the classified spy satellite inspection.
story: On April 12, 1981, NASA launched Space Shuttle Columbia on STS-1—the first time American astronauts rode a brand-new spacecraft without an uncrewed test flight. But right at liftoff, the ignition of the solid rocket boosters created an intense acoustic overpressure wave that bounced off the pad and slammed back into Columbia. The violent shockwave ripped off 16 thermal protection tiles and damaged 148 more. In orbit, astronauts John Young and Bob Crippen spotted missing tiles, raising fears the orbiter could burn up during reentry. Because the heat shield underside was blind to the crew, NASA initiated a secret operation with the National Reconnaissance Office, whose very existence was classified. Mission controllers aligned Columbia with a classified KH-11 spy satellite to photograph the tiles from space. The secret images confirmed the critical heat shield had held, allowing Columbia to land safely at Edwards Air Force Base.
angle: When the first Space Shuttle launched with humans aboard, an unexpected ignition shockwave stripped 16 heat tiles—forcing NASA to call in a top-secret spy satellite from a classified agency to see if the crew would burn up on reentry.

claims.claim: STS-1 was the inaugural orbital test flight of NASA's Space Shuttle program.
Space Shuttle Columbia lifted off on the STS-1 mission on April 12, 1981.
The mission was crewed by two astronauts: Commander John W. Young and Pilot Robert L. Crippen.
STS-1 was the first time an American crewed spacecraft launched on an orbital maiden flight without a prior uncrewed test flight.
An initial STS-1 launch attempt two days earlier on April 10, 1981, was scrubbed due to a computer glitch.
Columbia's launch coincided with the 20th anniversary of Yuri Gagarin's flight on Vostok 1.
At liftoff, ignition of the solid rocket boosters generated an unexpected acoustic overpressure shockwave that reflected off the launch pad.
The overpressure shockwave and launch forces tore 16 thermal protection tiles completely off Columbia.
A total of 148 thermal protection tiles were damaged during the launch.
To eliminate recurring overpressure shockwave damage on subsequent flights, NASA modified the pad's water sound suppression system.
Upon opening the payload bay doors in orbit, the crew visually spotted damage to the thermal protection tiles.
NASA secretly arranged to inspect Columbia's heat shield in orbit using an Air Force KH-11 KENNEN reconnaissance satellite.
In 1981, the very existence of the National Reconnaissance Office operating the spy satellites was classified.
While in orbit, the astronauts aboard Columbia caught sight of the KH-11 spy satellite passing in the distance.
The reconnaissance satellite images confirmed that damage to the orbiter's heat shield was not severe, clearing it for safe reentry.
Columbia touched down at Edwards Air Force Base in California on April 14, 1981.
Columbia landed on lake bed Runway 23 at Edwards Air Force Base.
The total duration of the STS-1 mission was 2 days, 6 hours, 20 minutes, and 53 seconds.
Pilot Robert Crippen compared the experience of liftoff to a catapult shot off an aircraft carrier.
After rollout, John Young remarked over the radio that Columbia was the world's greatest all-electric flying machine.
NASA described STS-1 as the boldest test flight in history.
The only payload flown on STS-1 was the Developmental Flight Instrumentation package to record flight stresses and vehicle performance.

disputed: Tile loss location: Source S1 states 16 undensified tiles were lost near the OMS pods, whereas source S5 states 16 tiles were missing from Columbia's underside; scripts should state 16 tiles were lost without specifying the location.

Orbit tally: Source S1 notes both 36 and 37 orbits in different sections, whereas source S2 lists 37 revolutions; scripts should cite the flight duration (2 days, 6 hours) or attribute the orbit count.

Body flap deflection and emergency ejection risk: Source S1 claims the shockwave forced the body flap past expected hydraulic failure limits and that Young said they would have ejected had they known, but sources S2, S3, and S5 mention only tile damage; scripts should leave out the body flap claim because it appears on only one site.
